title: Human Body
blurb: How your heart, brain, gut, immune system and senses work.

cards.title: A double pump
cards.text: The heart is two pumps side by side. The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen; the left side pumps it around the whole body.

cards.title: The circuit
cards.text: Blood makes a figure of eight: body → right heart → lungs → left heart → body. One full lap takes under a minute at rest.

cards.title: A lifetime of beats
cards.text: At around 70 beats per minute, the heart beats about 100,000 times a day and some 2.5–3 billion times in a lifetime.

cards.title: Arteries, veins, capillaries
cards.text: Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure. Veins bring it back, with valves to stop it flowing backwards. Tiny capillaries in between swap oxygen and waste with cells.

cards.title: What's in blood
cards.text: Blood is a little over half plasma (water, salts, proteins) and the rest mostly red blood cells, with white cells and platelets.

cards.title: Red blood cells
cards.text: Red cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein that makes blood red. They have no nucleus, live about 120 days, and you make about 2 million every second.

cards.title: Blood pressure
cards.text: Blood pressure has two numbers: systolic (as the heart squeezes) and diastolic (as it relaxes). A typical healthy reading is around 120/80 mmHg.

cards.title: Blood types
cards.text: Your blood type, A, B, AB or O, depends on markers on red cells; Rh positive or negative adds another. O negative can be given to almost anyone in an emergency.

cards.title: The heartbeat's spark
cards.text: Each beat starts in the sinoatrial node, the heart's natural pacemaker, which sends an electrical pulse across the heart. An ECG records that electricity.

cards.title: Take your pulse
cards.text: Press two fingers on the inside of your wrist below the thumb. Count beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4. Resting rates of 60–100 are typical for adults.

quiz.q: Where does the right side of the heart pump blood?
Which vessels have valves to stop backflow?
quiz.explain: Blood in veins is under low pressure.

lessons.title: The brain and nerves
lessons.summary: 86 billion neurons and how they talk.

cards.title: Neurons
cards.text: The brain has about 86 billion nerve cells. Each neuron receives signals through branches called dendrites and sends them along a long axon to other neurons.

cards.title: Electric and chemical
cards.text: Inside a neuron, signals travel as electrical pulses, up to about 120 m/s. Between neurons, at the synapse, they cross as chemicals called neurotransmitters.

cards.title: Brain regions
cards.text: The cerebrum handles thinking, senses and movement; the cerebellum coordinates balance; the brainstem runs breathing and heartbeat automatically.

cards.title: Four lobes
cards.text: The cerebrum's cortex has four lobes on each side, each with main jobs, though most tasks use many areas working together.

cards.title: Left and right

items.r: Both halves work together in everyone

cards.text: Each half of the brain controls the opposite side of the body. The idea of "left-brained logical" and "right-brained creative" people is a myth; both halves work together.

cards.title: The 10% myth

items.w: We only use 10% of our brain
items.r: We use virtually all of it

cards.text: We don't use only 10% of our brain. Scans show activity all over the brain across a day, and damage to almost any area causes problems.

cards.title: Energy hungry
cards.text: The brain is about 2% of body weight but uses roughly 20% of the body's energy, mostly to keep neurons ready to fire.

cards.title: Reflexes
cards.text: Touch a hot pan and your hand pulls back before you feel pain. Reflexes travel through the spinal cord without waiting for the brain, saving precious milliseconds.

cards.title: Neuroplasticity
cards.text: The brain rewires itself throughout life. Learning a skill strengthens connections between neurons that fire together; unused ones weaken.

cards.title: Learning to juggle
cards.text: Studies found that adults who learnt to juggle for three months showed growth in brain areas that track moving objects, which shrank back when they stopped.

quiz.q: How many neurons does the human brain have, roughly?
What part of the brain coordinates balance?
Do we use only 10% of our brain?
options: No, we use virtually all of it

lessons.title: Food and digestion
lessons.summary: From your plate to your cells.

cards.title: The journey
cards.text: Food travels through about 9 metres of digestive tract, from mouth to exit, over roughly one to three days.

cards.title: Mouth and teeth
cards.text: Teeth grind food and saliva starts digesting starch. Chewing well means less work for the stomach.

cards.title: The stomach
cards.text: The stomach churns food with strong acid (pH around 1.5–3.5) and enzymes that break down protein. Mucus protects its own lining from being digested.

cards.title: Small intestine
cards.text: Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine. Its lining is covered with tiny finger-like villi, giving a huge surface area.

cards.title: Large intestine
cards.text: The large intestine absorbs water and salt and is home to trillions of gut bacteria that help digest fibre and make some vitamins.

cards.title: The microbiome
cards.text: Your gut holds about as many bacterial cells as you have human cells. A varied diet with fibre feeds a varied microbiome.

cards.title: Three macronutrients
cards.text: Food gives energy from carbohydrates, fats and proteins. Fat has more than twice the energy per gram.

cards.title: The liver
cards.text: The liver is the body's chemical factory: it processes nutrients, stores energy as glycogen, makes bile to digest fat and breaks down toxins and alcohol.

cards.title: Feeling full
cards.text: After eating, stretch sensors and hormones signal fullness, but it takes about 20 minutes to register. Eating slowly helps you notice it in time.

cards.title: Water
cards.text: Adults need roughly 1.5–2 litres of fluids a day from drinks, more in heat or exercise. About 20% of our water comes from food.

quiz.explain: Its villi give a huge surface.

quiz.q: Which nutrient has the most energy per gram?

cards.title: Lines of defence
cards.text: The body defends in layers: barriers keep germs out, the innate system attacks anything foreign quickly, and the adaptive system learns specific enemies.

cards.title: Barriers
cards.text: Skin, mucus, tears, stomach acid and coughing all stop most germs before they get inside.

cards.title: Inflammation
cards.text: When germs get in, the area becomes red, warm, swollen and sore. Blood vessels widen to bring in defending cells: it's a sign the immune system is working.

cards.title: White blood cells
cards.text: Several kinds of white blood cells share the work: some swallow invaders, some make antibodies, and some destroy infected cells.

cards.title: Antibodies
cards.text: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins that lock onto one specific invader, like a key in a lock, marking it for destruction.

cards.title: Immune memory
cards.text: After an infection, memory cells stay for years. If the same germ returns, the body responds faster and stronger, often before you feel ill.

cards.title: Vaccines
cards.text: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless piece or version of a germ, so it builds memory without having the disease. Edward Jenner made the first vaccine, against smallpox, in 1796.

cards.title: Herd immunity
cards.text: When enough people are immune, a germ can't spread easily, protecting those who can't be vaccinated, like newborns. Smallpox was eradicated worldwide in 1980.

cards.title: Bacteria vs viruses
cards.text: Bacteria are living cells that antibiotics can kill. Viruses are much smaller and hijack our cells to copy themselves; antibiotics don't work on them.

cards.title: Fever
cards.text: A fever is the body turning up its thermostat. Higher temperature slows many germs and speeds up immune cells.

quiz.q: Do antibiotics work against viruses like the flu?

lessons.title: Senses and skeleton
lessons.summary: How you sense the world and hold yourself up.

cards.title: More than five senses
cards.text: Besides sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch, you sense balance, temperature, pain and the position of your limbs (proprioception), which lets you touch your nose with eyes closed.

cards.title: How eyes see
cards.text: Light enters through the cornea and lens, which focus an upside-down image on the retina. The brain flips it and builds the picture we see.

cards.title: Rods and cones
cards.text: The retina has rods for dim light and movement, and cones for colour. Three kinds of cones sense red, green and blue light.

cards.title: How ears hear
cards.text: Sound waves make the eardrum vibrate. Three tiny bones pass the vibration to the fluid-filled cochlea, where hair cells turn it into nerve signals.

cards.title: Taste is mostly smell
cards.text: The tongue detects five basic tastes; most "flavour" actually comes from smell. That's why food tastes bland with a blocked nose.

cards.title: The skeleton
cards.text: Adults have 206 bones; babies have about 300, which fuse as they grow. More than half of them are in the hands and feet.

cards.title: Bones are alive
cards.text: Bones are living tissue that constantly rebuild. They store calcium, and the marrow inside makes blood cells. Exercise and weight-bearing make bones stronger.

cards.title: Muscles
cards.text: There are about 600 muscles. Skeletal muscles can only pull, never push, so they work in pairs, like the biceps and triceps.

cards.title: Three types of muscle
cards.text: Skeletal muscles move bones by choice; smooth muscle moves food and blood vessels automatically; cardiac muscle in the heart never tires.

cards.title: Smallest and largest
cards.text: The smallest bone is the stirrup in the ear, about 3 mm. The largest is the thigh bone, the femur, roughly a quarter of your height.

quiz.q: How many bones does an adult have?
Why does food taste bland with a cold?
quiz.explain: The nose does most of the work.
